item.title: Bridgewater Raises $2B AI Fund While Warns of 18% Labor Dislocation
item.description:
Bridgewater Raises $2B AI Fund While Warns of 18% Labor Dislocation

Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s largest hedge funds, has raised almost $2 billion for an AI‑driven fund and publicly warned that AI could dislocate a substantial portion of the U.S. labor market.

🔍 Overview

  • “The latest harbinger of technological upheaval is Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s largest hedge funds.”
  • In 2024, Bridgewater raised almost $2 billion for an AI‑driven fund designed to let technology generate investment insights while humans manage the risk.
  • The firm says the AI fund has consistently beaten the market and produces ideas that differ from its traditional human traders.
  • “That just blows your mind thinking what the future holds,” Bar Dea said.

📊 Potential Labor Impact

  • “According to Bridgewater Chief Executive Officer Nir Bar Dea, AI could dislocate nearly one‑fifth of the US labor market if society fails to prepare and regulators don’t step in.”
  • “Our estimate is that AI can dislocate 18% of American labor.”
  • “So think about the magnitude of the societal breakdown that could happen.”

🏢 Bridgewater’s Internal Perspective

Person Role Quote
Nir Bar Dea Chief Executive Officer “If you’re going to build and understand how the world works, you want to combine humans and technology,” Bar Dea explained.
Greg Jensen Managing Chief Investment Officer “Managing Chief Investment Officer Greg Jensen—notably one of the earliest backers of OpenAI and Anthropic PBC—likened the current complacency around AI to the earliest days of the pandemic, when the public largely failed to appreciate the looming risks of Covid‑19.”
Nir Bar Dea CEO (additional) “Bar Dea is far from the only executive at the $100 billion firm waving a red flag.”

🚀 AI‑Driven Fund Performance

  • The AI fund “has consistently beaten the market while generating entirely different ideas than Bridgewater’s traditional human traders.”
  • Bar Dea notes that off‑the‑shelf technology is not sufficient: “You have to have unique data, unique trainers” to maintain an edge.

⚠️ Cautions & Risks

  • Anthropic warned about potentially severe consequences from AI in a filing this week.
  • Paul Tudor Jones described the approaching AI threat as being “like waiting for a Category 6 hurricane.”
  • Elon Musk, who previously warned that developing AI was akin to “summoning the demon,” said at the White House that “Jobs are going to change. Jobs have always changed.” He expects an evolution of roles rather than catastrophe.

💡 Why it matters

  • Bridgewater’s dual approach—massive capital allocation to AI in investing while publicly flagging macro‑economic labor risks—highlights the growing convergence of finance, technology, and policy concerns.
  • The firm’s statement that technology is crucial for its global macroeconomic investments underscores the strategic importance of AI across the financial sector.
  • The range of perspectives—from warnings of labor dislocation to optimism about an “age of abundance”—reflects the broader debate on AI’s societal impact.

#AI #Finance #LaborEconomics #Bridgewater

Source: Another day, another AI warning: Bridgewater sounds the alarm on 18% labor shock

item.title: New ISO Standard Guides AI System Impact Assessments
item.description:
New ISO Standard Guides AI System Impact Assessments

Researchers and industry proponents are focusing on a key role in the AI workforce—‘facilitators’—who translate AI capability into practical deployment. To support this group, attention is being drawn to the new international standard ISO/IEC 42005:2025, which provides guidance on systematically integrating AI system impact assessments into an organization’s broader governance ecosystem.

🔍 Overview

With generative AI adoption moving faster than the personal computer or the internet and global AI-related investment in 2025 representing $581.69 billion, organizations must position their workforce to use AI responsibly. Researchers affiliated with the AI Adoption Initiative argue that the workforce relates to AI through an AI Labor Stack comprised of AI innovators, facilitators, and users. Facilitators are often ’the missing middle’ in national AI strategies, though they are responsible for translating AI capability into practical deployment across firms, sectors, and public services. The new ISO standard aims to support this facilitator population.

🧩 Key Features of ISO/IEC 42005

  • Provides explicit guidance on how to integrate AI system impact assessments into existing impact assessment processes within an enterprise, which often include different kinds of impact assessments for IT systems (e.g., risk, privacy, cybersecurity).
  • Unlocks a more integrated AI governance process for customers.
  • Specifies the specific information that should be documented in an AI system impact assessment via a templated assessment approach.
  • Explains how to leverage other risk assessments the enterprise may already be conducting to avoid duplication.

⚙️ How It Works

The standard covers the full assessment life cycle, including:

  • Scoping and execution
  • Analysis and reporting
  • Ongoing monitoring and review

It also identifies:

  • When an AI system impact assessment should be conducted
  • How comprehensive it should be
  • How to establish reassessment triggers

When establishing the timing for assessment and reassessment, the standard recommends considering triggers such as:

  • Applicable legal requirements
  • Contractual obligations
  • Internal policies
  • Customer expectations
  • Changes to the AI system, its operational environment, or its context
  • Other factors

The standard explains how to conduct a lighter AI system impact assessment triage—a quick classification to identify whether a more comprehensive assessment is needed or not (depending on level of risk)—before committing to a full assessment or reassessment.

💡 Why It Matters

An AI system impact assessment is a documented process of AI system risk identification by which organizations developing, providing, or using AI systems consider impacts to the organization, individuals, communities, groups, and societies. The process channels its outputs, such as identification of privacy impacts, discriminatory impacts, or performance impacts, into the organization’s risk management decisions. Using an AI system impact assessment process helps organizations responsibly manage their AI deployments, choosing appropriate guardrails to manage identified risks. AI system impact assessments are an integral part of an organization’s overall risk management process.

🚀 Practical Implementation Options

The standard provides two approaches:

Approach Description
Integrated (Annex D) Provides a process organizations can use to simplify impact assessments and avoid duplication, helping coordinate relevant reviews (e.g., risk, legal, security, privacy, procurement, or architecture).
Standalone (Annex E) Provides a ready-to-use template for self-contained implementation.

Organizations such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) offer tools to support governance work aligned with ISO/IEC 42005 and other responsible AI best practices, including an ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management Systems (AIMS) implementation guide on AWS and the Well-Architected Framework: Responsible AI Lens.

#ISO42005 #AIGovernance #ResponsibleAI #AIRiskManagement #AICompliance

Source: Responsible AI governance: How AWS positions customers to align with ISO/IEC 42005:2025 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Qualys TotalAppSec Achieves FedRAMP High Authorization
item.description:
Qualys TotalAppSec Achieves FedRAMP High Authorization

🔎 Overview

Qualys TotalAppSec has been granted FedRAMP High authorization on the Qualys Government Platform (FedRAMP Certified Class D, package FR2231052341). The authorization positions the service within the federal high‑impact security boundary and enables agencies to use its continuous application‑security capabilities.

⚙️ What TotalAppSec Provides

  • Maintains 99.2%+ CISA KEV coverage with a 16‑hour median from CVE disclosure to detection.
  • Generates ATO and Continuous Monitoring (ConMon) evidence from within an authorized High boundary.
  • Detects and reports vulnerabilities at a cadence that meets the daily detection requirement for High‑impact assets.
  • Supports application‑layer asset tagging as required by CISA BOD 26‑04.

📜 Policy and Compliance Backdrop

  • NIST SP 800‑228 (updated March 2026) treats APIs as a distinct control surface, calling for inventories that include shadow and zombie APIs, runtime discovery, and reconciliation of declared specs against live traffic.
  • CISA BOD 26‑04 (issued June 10 2026) mandates risk‑based remediation and application‑layer asset tagging by December 7 2026. The directive replaces flat patch deadlines with urgency calculations that factor in exposure, KEV status, exploit automation, and technical impact.
  • For High‑impact findings, agencies must assess reachability and exploitability for each finding and conduct at‑least‑daily detection.
  • Non‑compliant offerings lose their authorization after March 7 2027, removing the right to sell to the government.

📈 Security Impact

  • Mean Time to Exploit (MTTE) is now estimated at minus seven days (M‑Trends 2026), indicating adversaries often act before a vulnerability is disclosed.
  • Agencies cannot out‑patch an adversary who starts before disclosure, underscoring the need for rapid detection.
  • Public‑facing applications are now the leading initial‑access vector (40 % of incidents) and 56 % of tracked vulnerabilities require no authentication to exploit.
  • Federal AI use cases have more than doubled to 3,611 across 56 agencies, with 445 designated high‑impact AI subject to OMB M‑25‑21 risk‑management practices. AI coding assistants have cleared FedRAMP authorization, and the GSA is asking agencies to build Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

🚀 Availability and Next Steps

  • TotalAppSec’s FedRAMP High status enables immediate use by federal agencies seeking to meet the CISA BOD 26‑04 remediation timeline.
  • Agencies should integrate TotalAppSec into their application‑layer asset tagging processes and ensure continuous API discovery to satisfy NIST SP 800‑228 requirements.
  • Ongoing monitoring will be required to maintain daily detection and reporting compliance through the December 7 2026 deadline and beyond.

#FedRAMP #GovSec #APIsecurity #AICompliance

Source: Qualys TotalAppSec Is Now FedRAMP High Authorized | Qualys

item.title: AI Governance Climbs to Boardroom Fiduciary Duty
item.description:
AI Governance Climbs to Boardroom Fiduciary Duty

As boards push for fast AI adoption, a new question is emerging: what happens to human judgment when AI is everywhere? University of Chicago President Paul Alivisatos argued in The Wall Street Journal that students should learn to think with AI, without AI, and about AI. The shift is moving AI governance from a technical issue to a board-level priority, much like cybersecurity did a decade ago.

🔍 Overview

AI governance is now a fiduciary responsibility. The boardroom question is no longer “How do we deploy AI?” but “How do we scale AI innovation while protecting trust, accountability, and long-term enterprise value?” Organizations with trustworthy AI foundations move faster than those retrofitting controls after an incident.

🧩 Key Details

  • Only 28% of talent management leaders believe they have high-potential talent in their most critical roles (Gartner research).
  • AI can make a workforce highly efficient and quietly less capable of independent judgment.
  • The winners of the next decade won’t be the companies with the most AI tools.
  • They’ll be the ones whose leaders know when to trust AI, when to challenge it, and when to override it.
  • Bias, misinformation, security gaps, and regulatory exposure are not solved after the fact.

⚙️ Governance Requirements

  • Require governance models with clear ownership, auditability, and escalation paths from day one.
  • Before autonomy scales, require management to show controls on agent authority, access, data movement, and runtime monitoring.
  • Name decision stewards who have the authority to challenge, pause, or override AI when value, trust, or regulatory obligations are at stake.

💡 Why It Matters

History won’t remember who adopted AI first. It will remember who deployed it responsibly — and turned governance into a competitive advantage. Trust isn’t an ethical footnote anymore; it’s a strategic asset. AI safety is fast becoming a board fiduciary duty. The US and China are setting up channels to contain AI-related incidents before they escalate, because AI accelerates insight and amplifies mistakes at machine speed. The next AI risk isn’t what models know — it’s what agents are authorized to do.

Pillar Role
Cost Sustainable AI value
Cybersecurity Sustainable AI value
Trustworthiness Sustainable AI value

Safety isn’t the brake. It’s the accelerator.

#AIGovernance #FiduciaryDuty #BoardroomAI #TrustworthyAI #AISafety

Source: Khwaja’s Take: Who Owns the Outcome When AI Acts? + Nitin Nohria’s “The CEO” and Where I’m Speaking Next.

item.title: Wealth Management AI Progress Stalls Without Strong Backend Infrastructure
item.description:
Wealth Management AI Progress Stalls Without Strong Backend Infrastructure

The Wealth Mosaic’s AI in Wealth 2026: APAC conference in Singapore on 24 September highlighted that the wealth‑management industry’s rapid move from digitalisation to artificial intelligence is now hitting a bottleneck: the surrounding systems, processes and human relationships.

📈 Industry Momentum

  • The sector has “moved quickly from digitalisation to artificial intelligence (AI)” but the next stage “may depend less on the capabilities of the technology itself than on the systems, processes and human relationships around it.”
  • This theme recurred throughout the morning sessions at the event.

⚙️ Infrastructure Gap

  • Kaushik Kadayam, Executive Director at Standard Chartered, opened the event warning that “AI is great – but AI needs a robust backend workflow and operations and technology is important.”
  • He likened the situation to “lifting a lot more on the right arm and we’re really bulking it up here. But the left arm is still very skimpy and skinny.”
  • He said sophisticated AI can only take firms so far if “processes beneath them remain fragmented or manual.”
  • Legacy systems that “lack APIs” and manual information transfers still dominate many firms.
  • The uneven spread of technology means markets such as Singapore, Hong Kong and London are ahead, while “greenfield markets where technology adoption remains less advanced could offer more scope for genuinely transformative applications.”
  • Risk appetite is a further challenge: client confidentiality, data restrictions, regulators, compliance and risk teams must be comfortable with the technology.
  • Consequently, “much current technology investment is going towards the foundations required for transformation rather than AI alone.”
  • Kadayam estimated that “around 90 percent of banking technology investment is still directed towards upgrading technology, moving to the cloud, and ‘getting the basics right’ – leaving a much smaller proportion for transformation.”
  • He sees the opportunity to shift from isolated AI use cases to “end‑to‑end processes” and predicts firms will “automate the entire process front‑to‑back with AI.”
  • Yet he stresses that automation will not remove the relationship element: “The fact that we still need relationship managers, and we don’t have AI talking to clients, signifies that trust is the biggest win here.”

🤖 AI Use Cases & Caution

  • Tawishi Singh, Head of Partnerships & Channels at Keenai, sees clear internal productivity gains from AI but advises a cautious rollout to clients: “Do we want to necessarily be the first one to be out there doing it? No, because I think we’d rather tread carefully than necessarily be the first one out and doing it wrong.”
  • She notes that adoption takes time because of “data, risk governance, regulation, people, education, and differing levels of enthusiasm across an organisation.”
  • Singh adds, “I don’t care about the speed necessarily. I care that it’s accurate and achieves the results.”
  • She highlights portfolio generation and analysis as proven internal uses, while emphasizing that “ultimately the human has to assess it.”
  • Singh also points to risk and compliance as a productivity use case where AI can handle repetitive work, freeing specialists for higher‑value tasks.
  • Yee (name only) identifies portfolio reporting, reconciliations and document review as areas where technology can deliver “substantial efficiency gains while maintaining human oversight.”
  • Yee urges vendors to stop selling AI‑enabled software without first defining the pain point, asking “What is it they are actually solving for? Is this three hours saved or not?”
  • He warns against merely “dressing up the same chatbots with AI conversation” when AI is added to existing processes without real improvement.

🤝 Human Relationship & Trust

  • Kadayam stresses that firms must continue to win client trust and keep customers informed as new AI‑driven processes are introduced.
  • In a fireside chat, Nicole Teo (Vice President Marketing, Lighthouse Canton) and Mark Yeo Tee Shen (Head of Investment Advisory, StashAway) discussed AI’s potential to personalise marketing and client interactions, but cautioned that excessive personalisation could erode trust if clients feel “they are being watched too closely.”

🚀 Path Forward

  • The consensus at the conference is that the wealth‑management industry must first solidify its backend workflow, APIs and data governance before AI can deliver end‑to‑end automation.
  • Successful transformation will blend robust infrastructure, selective internal AI use cases, and a continued focus on relationship‑manager‑led trust with clients.
Speaker Focus Area
Kaushik Kadayam (Standard Chartered) Need for robust backend workflow; 90 % of tech spend on basics
Tawishi Singh (Keenai) Internal productivity; cautious client‑facing rollout
Yee (unspecified) Efficiency in reporting, reconciliations, document review; vendor skepticism
Nicole Teo & Mark Yeo Tee Shen (Lighthouse Canton & StashAway) AI‑driven personalisation vs trust risk

#WealthTech #AI #FinTech #RiskManagement

Source: The Wealth Mosaic

item.title: TAISE Framework Repurposes AI Weather Models for Catastrophe Risk Modeling
item.description:
TAISE Framework Repurposes AI Weather Models for Catastrophe Risk Modeling

A new study proposes the TAISE framework, which utilizes AI weather forecasting models to generate extreme weather sequences for catastrophe (CAT) risk modeling.

🧩 How it works

  • Model Repurposing: The framework repurposes AI weather forecasting models to produce coherent extreme weather sequences.
  • Self-Iterative Generation: TAISE uses self-iterative generation to produce continuous global atmospheric fields, allowing extreme events to emerge.

💡 Why it matters

  • Cost Reduction: A proof-of-concept experiment showed an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared to conventional methods.
  • Improved Continuity: The framework captures temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations, which are absent in snapshot-based approaches.
  • Modernization: Traditional CAT risk models have relied on costly manual construction for weather scenarios, an approach largely unchanged since the 1990s.

#AI #WeatherForecasting #RiskModeling #TAISE

Source: From Manual Construction to AI-Driven Scenario Emergence: Rethinking Catastrophe Risk Modeling
